title: Envoy & Sidecar Proxy Mechanics
summary: What the proxy in "sidecar proxy" is actually doing, using Envoy — the proxy most meshes are built on — as the reference.

slides.markdown:
**Envoy** is the proxy most service meshes (Istio, Consul) are built on — a single, battle-tested data-plane component reused across many mesh products.

- Its config model is **listeners → routes → clusters**: where to accept traffic, how to match it, and where to send it.
- Traffic gets into the sidecar via kernel-level redirection (**iptables** or **eBPF**) — no app code changes.
- It gets its configuration dynamically from a control plane via **xDS**, not a static file.

slides.subTitle: The proxy most meshes are built on
slides.markdown:
**Envoy** is a high-performance L4/L7 proxy written in C++, originally built at Lyft, that became the de facto standard data-plane proxy — Istio, Consul, and many gateways all run Envoy underneath, configured differently.

This matters because it means "how a mesh works" and "how Envoy works" are largely the same question: the mesh product (Istio) is mostly a **control plane** wrapped around the same Envoy binary running as every sidecar.

slides.subTitle: Envoy's core configuration model
slides.markdown:
Envoy's configuration has three core building blocks: a **listener** defines where Envoy accepts connections (an IP:port); a **route** matches an incoming request (by path, header, etc.) to a destination; a **cluster** is the actual group of upstream endpoints (e.g. all healthy pods of the `orders` service) Envoy load-balances across.

A request's path through this model: it arrives at a **listener**, gets matched by a **route**, and is forwarded to a **cluster** — the same three-stage shape whether the proxy is a gateway or a sidecar.

![How traffic actually gets redirected into the sidecar via iptables or eBPF](assets/sidecar-traffic-redirect.svg)

The application makes a normal outbound call with no awareness of the mesh. At the kernel level, **iptables NAT rules** (traditional approach) or an **eBPF program** (newer, lower-overhead approach) silently redirect that traffic through the sidecar's listener first — the app's socket calls are unchanged.

slides.subTitle: How Envoy gets configuration dynamically
slides.markdown:
**xDS** (the family of discovery service APIs — LDS, RDS, CDS, EDS for listeners, routes, clusters, endpoints) is how Envoy receives its configuration **live**, from the control plane, instead of a static file loaded at startup. When a routing rule changes, the control plane pushes updated config over xDS and Envoy applies it **without a restart or dropped connections**.

This dynamic-config model is what makes mesh-wide changes — a new canary weight, a rotated certificate — propagate to thousands of proxies in seconds, instead of requiring a rolling redeploy of every service.

slides.subTitle: The sidecar's latency isn't free
slides.markdown:
"The sidecar is transparent, so it's basically free" is a common but wrong assumption. Every request now makes **two extra hops** — through the caller's sidecar and the callee's sidecar — each adding real, measurable latency (typically low single-digit milliseconds per hop, more under load).

For most services this overhead is negligible next to the benefits (mTLS, retries, observability). But for a handful of latency-critical paths in a large system, that stacked overhead across many hops in a call chain is a genuine cost worth measuring, not assuming away.
